oneliner.t: Birmingham Democrat and former public-finance lawyer who has represented Alabama's 7th District since January 2011 and sits on the Ways and Means Committee.

born.t: January 1, 1965, Huntsville, Alabama (Wikipedia only; not confirmed in a second source)

upbringing.t: Raised in Selma. Her father, Andrew A. Sewell, was a high-school basketball coach; her mother, Nancy Gardner Sewell, was a high-school librarian and later a Selma city council member. Wikipedia says she was Selma High School's first Black valedictorian. After Princeton, Oxford (Marshall Scholar) and Harvard Law, she clerked for Chief U.S. District Judge U.W. Clemon in Birmingham, practiced securities law at Davis Polk & Wardwell in New York, and returned to Alabama in 2004 as a public-finance lawyer at Maynard, Cooper & Gale. The family and early-life details rest on Wikipedia alone in this research.

education.deg: M.A. (Marshall Scholar; Wikipedia lists the Oxford degree as a bachelor's in political science)

career.role: Law clerk to Chief Judge U.W. Clemon

platform.t: Lead sponsor of the Voting Rights Advancement Act, later renamed the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act; backs expanded early voting.
Supports Medicaid expansion and incentives for states to adopt it. Backs bills to lower prescription-drug costs, fund rural hospitals and study health disparities.
Supports abortion rights; opposed Alabama's Human Life Protection Act and the 2022 Dobbs decision.
Her 2014 campaign site listed education, health care, and jobs and the economy as her issues.

claims.claim: Graduated from Princeton (1986), studied at Oxford as a Marshall Scholar (1988) and earned a Harvard law degree (1992).

said.where: Biography as reported (Ballotpedia, Wikipedia); campaign about page unreachable

record.t: Ballotpedia and Wikipedia agree on all three schools and years. The Marshall Scholarship appears only in Wikipedia. No registrar records checked.

record.t: Oct 8 update: Wikipedia, citing the congress.gov bill record, says she introduced H.R. 4, the Voting Rights Advancement Act, on Feb. 26, 2019. The Clerk's roll call confirms H.R. 4 passed the House 228–187 on Dec. 6, 2019 (she voted Aye). The House later agreed to H.Con.Res. 107 renaming it for John Lewis. The sponsor line itself could not be opened on congress.gov (blocked to the fetch tool); verdict changed from unverifiable to true on this basis.

claims.claim: Sponsored a 2019 bill, which passed, providing $70 million to historically Black colleges.

said.where: Legislative biography as reported (Wikipedia); congress.gov blocked

record.t: Stated by Wikipedia. The congress.gov bill record and enacted-law text were not reached.

said.t: Cosponsored the STOCK Act, the 2011–12 congressional insider-trading and disclosure law.

did.t: Voted Nay on H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would bar members from buying new individual stocks. The House text also carried SAVE America Act voter photo-ID provisions, which Democrats cited in opposing it. She bought Apple and Nvidia shares in April 2025 and sold GE HealthCare and Tapestry shares in March 2026, all reported on PTRs.

said.t: Supports Medicaid expansion and health-coverage programs; voted for the ACA.

did.t: Voted Yea on H.R. 1834, the three-year extension of enhanced ACA premium tax credits (passed 230–196).

said.t: Sponsored the Voting Rights Advancement Act; backs expanded early voting.

did.t: Voted Nay on the SAVE Act (H.R. 8281 in 2024; H.R. 22 in 2025), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register.

entries.t: One of 48 House Democrats who voted for the Laken Riley Act's first House version (and one of 46 who backed the Senate-amended S. 5).

aipac_endorse.t: Not confirmed — Track AIPAC shows no AIPAC-endorsement label for her (as of 2026-10-08); AIPAC's own endorsement page was not checked.

votes.bill: H.R. 8034 Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act
votes.what: About $26 billion in emergency funding for Israel's missile defense, U.S. regional operations and humanitarian aid including for Gaza (CBO ~$26.4B); passed 366–58 and later enacted inside H.R. 815.
Directs the Education Department to use the IHRA working definition of antisemitism in Title VI enforcement; passed 320–91, not taken up by the Senate.

votes.what: Would require sanctions on International Criminal Court officials who investigate or prosecute U.S. or allied (including Israeli) protected persons; passed 243–140.

history.approx_note: FEC page rendering gave PAC money as 'about $1.68 million' and individuals as 'about $666,000'; exact figures not captured

fec.history_note: Cycles 2012–2020 were not retrieved; the tool's per-request budget and FEC HTTP 429 rate limits made sequential fetching impractical. Ballotpedia's OpenSecrets-derived table for 2009–2014 shows $4,205,678 raised and $3,714,796 spent; top industries were lawyers/law firms ($659,788), securities & investment ($249,000), insurance ($205,800) and commercial banks ($164,700). In documented cycles, PAC ('other committee') money grew from about 20% of receipts (2010) to about 68% (2024) and 81% (2025–Jul 22, 2026). 'other' in 2026 = receipts minus individual and PAC contributions. Business vs. ideological PAC split not computed. Outside spending: none found in sources reached; FEC IE data not checked directly.

corp.t: Business and trade PAC money every documented cycle. FEC 'other committee' contributions were $357,855 (2010), about $1.68M (2022), $2,063,874 (2024) and $1,589,750 (2025–Jul 22, 2026; about 81% of receipts). ProPublica's 2023–25 itemized list shows about $10,000 each from the PACs of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama, UnitedHealth Group, CVS Health, Community Health Systems, American Hospital Association (~$9,000), Gilead Sciences (~$9,000), TIAA, PNC, Norfolk Southern and Vulcan Materials. Health insurers, providers and drugmakers fall under Ways and Means' Medicare/tax jurisdiction. In 2009–2014, per Ballotpedia's OpenSecrets data, securities & investment ($249,000), insurance and commercial banks were among her top industries (PAC plus individual money).

lobby.t: Track AIPAC lists $75,552 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC, AGG) and their large donors, and $0 in independent expenditures. ProPublica's itemized list shows roughly $13,400 in 2023–25 receipts listed as American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC PAC conduit), approximate.

trades.period: Apr 2025–Mar 2026 (two PTRs found); none in 2023 annual

note.t: Latest annual report found is for calendar 2023 (filed Aug 13, 2024 after an extension). Assets of $245K–$675K, mostly mutual funds in a Merrill Lynch IRA plus individual stocks: Tapestry ($50K–$100K), Cisco and GE. Liabilities of $315K–$800K: mortgages on Birmingham and D.C. homes, a co-op share loan and a $15K–$50K Citibank credit card. The homes themselves are not reportable assets, so the range understates net worth. Uncompensated positions: chair of the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation board, Princeton trustee, Stennis Center board. 2025–26 PTRs: bought Apple and Nvidia ($1K–$15K each) Apr 10, 2025. Sold GE HealthCare ($1K–$15K) and Tapestry ($15K–$50K) Mar 25, 2026. Apple and Nvidia are exposed to trade and tariff policy (she sits on the Trade subcommittee) but are not listed as overlap because the committee does not regulate those industries directly. Calendar 2024 and 2025 annual reports were not located; LegiStorm lists a 2025 annual and a 2026 extension letter.

committees: Ways and Means (Oversight; Social Security; Trade subcommittees)

revolving.t: Quiver Quantitative's lobbying-disclosure summary lists 7 former Sewell staffers who became registered lobbyists, representing 76 clients including 14 public companies. Not checked against Senate LDA records (blocked).

democracy.t: Not among the seven House Democrats who rose to object to 2016 electoral votes. The objections were ruled out of order for lack of a senator's signature, and there was no recorded vote.
Voted Nay on the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (Roll Call 10; failed 121–303).
Voted Nay on the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (Roll Call 11; failed 138–282).
Voted for the article of impeachment against President Trump after Jan. 6; the only Alabama House member to vote to impeach in both impeachments.

note.t: Raised in Selma, which is in AL-07, and lives in Birmingham. Coverage differs on her home city: Reflector and ADN say Birmingham, 1819 News says Hoover. Years of continuous district residence not documented; she practiced law in New York roughly 1994–2004.

checks.legal: Not done. CourtListener is blocked for this tool, Justia was not reached, Alacourt is paywalled, and no news search for lawsuits or charges was possible (the shared web-search budget ran out). House Ethics and OCC/OCE pages were not fetched. Nothing turned up in the Wikipedia, Ballotpedia, Reflector or ADN material reviewed. ETHICS (Oct 8): The Office of Congressional Conduct (formerly OCE) referral list was read directly. Pages covering Oct 2009–Feb 2010 and Mar 2017–Mar 2026 list no referral naming Sewell. Pages for roughly 2010–2016 returned duplicate content and could not be read, so 2011–2016 is not confirmed from that source. ethics.house.gov was refused by the fetch tool. Wikipedia and Ballotpedia mention no ethics complaint, investigation or finding. New news searches could not be run.
checks.foreign: 2023 House annual disclosure: no foreign assets or income; one 2023 London trip listed under travel. FARA database blocked; not searched.
checks.claims: The mechanical sample could not be run: sewellforcongress.com (about and issues pages) could not be fetched (tool permission not granted), and no ad coverage was found within the search budget. Fallback: her biography and legislative claims as published by Ballotpedia and Wikipedia. Five checkable claims. Oct 8 pass: sewellforcongress.com was still blocked (Ballotpedia lists a contact address at terrisewellforcongress.com; also blocked), sewell.house.gov was refused, and Ballotpedia lists no 2026 ads or survey. Upgraded the VRAA authorship claim to true using the Clerk's H.R. 4 roll call and Wikipedia's congress.gov citation. Wikipedia names no bill for the $70 million HBCU claim, so that claim stays unverifiable. Total: 5 claims, 2 rated true, 3 unverifiable.
checks.democracy: Clerk of the House roll calls 10 and 11 (2021), read directly; CNN's Jan 6, 2017 list of objectors; Wikipedia (impeachment votes).

research_notes: MONEY: FEC figures are from committee C00458976 pages; the candidate page was rate-limited (HTTP 429). Coverage runs through Jul 22, 2026. Wikipedia's table shows $1,514,475 raised and $3,650,598 on hand through Mar 31, 2026. She has $3.75M on hand against a challenger with about $116K, much of it a $100K self-loan. ProPublica Itemizer PAC totals were summed by the reading tool from a long, truncated list (about June 2023–Nov 2025), so treat individual PAC amounts as approximate. COMMITTEES: Ways and Means membership is confirmed by Ballotpedia only; Wikipedia's committee list was not shown. DISCLOSURE: net worth uses the CY2023 report because later annual PDFs could not be located without the Clerk's search form, which needed a permission prompt that timed out. The negative low end comes from mortgages being listed while the homes are not. VOTES: key-vote roll calls are in al-votes.json; Israel-related ones are repeated in israel.votes. WEB LIMITS (Oct 8, 2026 pass): the shared web-search budget was used up, and outbound connections to campaign sites, web.archive.org, census.gov, bls.gov, congress.gov and the House Clerk's disclosure search were blocked or refused. ETHICS: set to 'done' after reading the OCC/OCE referral list directly, which shows no Sewell referral for 2017–2026 and 2009–10. A human should confirm the 2011–2016 pages, which wouldn't render distinct content, and check ethics.house.gov. CLAIMS: still only 2 rated verdicts. Her campaign and House sites were never reached, so the mechanical sample has not been run; checklist.claims stays 'news'. The Selma valedictorian, Maynard Cooper and Marshall Scholar claims cite the Washington Post, the Daily Princetonian and St Hilda's College per Wikipedia, but none of those pages could be opened.
